item.title: Cornell and the sexual counterrevolution
item.description: No, we don’t want a world before birth control
item.content:encoded:
By Maibritt Henkel

Consider the sticky situation of Sophie Baek, the heroine of Bridgerton’s fourth season. Despite being but a lowly housemaid, she and the aristocratic Benedict Bridgerton fall in love. One night, fire in their loins, they get carried away. The sex is passionate and consensual, but entirely verboten by Regency-era social norms: No lawful heir will come out of their cross-class, premarital affair.

This leaves Sophie in a state of terrible torment as she waits for her period. A swollen belly would be evidence of her transgression and leave her a ruined woman, not to mention a single mother.

While sexual norms have ebbed and flowed over the past 200 years, the dominant understanding of the social function of sex was pretty straightforward until relatively recently: Sex was for procreation. More precisely, it was for the procreation of legitimate children born within wedlock. This meant that sex was also for a very narrow segment of the population: married men and women.

If you weren’t having sex for the straightforwardly practical purpose of reproduction, then it meant you were doing it in the much more awkward, socially unproductive, and spiritually contentious pursuit of pleasure.

Share

Since the 1960s, it has become much easier to decouple sex from procreation. That was when birth control, a technology that might have saved 19th-century women like Sophie from pregnancy scares, became widely available in the United States, bringing with it new conventions around sex.

Today, most men will still marry you even if you’re not a virgin. Thanks to the technological and cultural intervention of the sexual revolution, the majority of Americans now have the freedom to think of pregnancy as an optional outcome of sex, rather than its primary function, which has opened the door to conversations about what else sex might be for. The relevant question for many women has become “Am I enjoying this?” instead of “Would my life be over if I got pregnant with this man’s baby?”

Not everyone views this as progress.

In The Case Against the Sexual Revolution, Louise Perry, a British columnist at The Wall Street Journal, argued that women were better off before contraception removed the risk of pregnancy. In her telling, decoupling sex from reproduction has produced a culture where men feel entitled to demand sex from women and women feel like they have no excuse not to give it to them.

Mary Harrington, contributing editor at Unherd and an intellectual ally of Perry’s, made the same point in her book Feminism Against Progress: “a woman who refuses birth control will be highly motivated to be choosy about her partners. Pregnancy risk is, after all, a cast-iron reason to reject having sex with anyone out of politeness.”

In short, removing procreation from the equation turned men into louts and women into pushovers. At a moment when young people really do seem to be struggling with romantic connection, this account has intuitive appeal. If men and women can’t even ask each other out on dates, how can they be expected to communicate their most intimate preferences and boundaries? It’s a daunting question.

But the answer does not lie in the past. If you take a longer view of gender relations, back to before the pill and the normalization of premarital sex, you will not find a golden age of mutually consensual and pleasurable heterosexual intimacy. All of us, most of all women, are better off when our sex lives are governed by consent and pleasure than by procreation and marital obligation.

Male entitlement existed before birth control

To critics of contraception and modern sex norms, the unfolding rape case at Cornell University — in which a college sophomore was allegedly pressured into taking drugs and then sexually assaulted by seven members of a fraternity — is further confirmation that the sexual revolution has paved the way for depraved men to have their way with hapless women.

In a recent essay in the Journal titled “How the Sexual Revolution Led to Cornell,” Perry wrote: “while the villains in this story are responsible for their own villainy, they were also set up to fail by a sexual culture that can’t help but produce tragedies like this.”

In other words: When you tell women that promiscuity is liberating and men that women are free to set the terms of their promiscuity, the outcome is a confused quagmire of coercion.

Perry advocates for the norms of the precontraception era, when “the community set restrictions on both male and female sexual behavior, not out of irrational prudishness or misogyny, but because unwise sexual encounters could very well lead to an unignorable outcome: the birth of a baby.” Even though technology has virtually eliminated that risk, it has not eliminated the need for a mechanism by which to protect women from men’s ravenous sexual appetites.

Here is where I agree with Harrington and Perry: Women should absolutely not be having sex out of politeness. Consent is clearly a necessary but insufficient arbiter of morally acceptable sex, as the Cornell case exemplifies. Even if the survivor in that case had verbally consented to the drugs and the group sex, that may not have exempted the household of men from moral wrongdoing. Power asymmetries always complicate the validity of consent.

Perry blames modern sex norms for what happened that night at the Chi Phi fraternity. To her, pamphlets on sexual pleasure and “workshops on sex toys” are part of the problem, for they contribute to the illusion that women have enough agency, and men enough self-control, to handle their own sexual freedom.

But to the extent that women still feel that they owe men sex, that is not the fault of the sexual revolution. If you want to talk about imperfect consent, then consider the sex that was had within lifelong marriages from roughly the Reformation to the mid-20th century.

With divorce being difficult, expensive, and a recipe for social ruin, women had very little leverage to shape their marriages’ sexual terms. And it wasn’t until 1993 that marital rape was outlawed in all 50 states. To be clear, that meant that, in states where it was legal, a husband legally could not be charged with raping his wife.

Subscribe now

Perry acknowledged this in her column: “of course rape still sometimes happened, including within marriage and within the family, since there has never been a culture free from sexual violence.”

This is an understatement. The position of the state was that women had no grounds to reject sex within marriage because procreation was the entire purpose of sex. Whether or not birth control emboldened some men to be more demanding of sex, pre-sexual-revolution marital rape laws legally entitled men to it.

Unlike Perry, I am not ready to give up on female agency — or male self-control, for that matter. Especially because I do not buy the story that the last six decades have been a failure on either front. When asked about their first sexual intercourse, the percentage of women who say they “really wanted it to happen at the time” rose from 34% in 2002 to 42% in 2011 to 2015.

Today there is at least some precedent for asking women what they want — and an increased propensity among men to respect it. Between 1995 and 2010, the rate of rape or sexual assault fell by well over half.

What conservatives owe the sexual revolution

A number of social conservatives anxious about the declining marriage rate have now taken to making the argument that married Americans have better sex than unmarried Americans. Brad Wilcox and Grant Bailey, who run the Get Married Initiative at the Institute for Family Studies, will have you know that “no group of Americans seems to be having more sex—and more satisfying sex—than married men and women who regularly attend a place of worship.” Similarly, Harrington contends that sex within marriage is better for women because the alternative is “casual hook-ups with a 10 percent chance of orgasm.”

The fact that right-wing intellectuals care about women reaching orgasm is wonderful. But that argument only has purchase because we are all fortunate enough to live in the aftermath of the sexual revolution.

Harrington makes the fair point that lifelong partners are more likely to care about “mutual pleasure.” But that is not a concept from the procreative lexicon for the simple reason that sex geared toward procreation does not require mutual pleasure. From a conception standpoint, the female orgasm serves absolutely no reproductive purpose.

At the risk of sounding uncouth: To say that sex is for having children within marriage is to say that sex is for male ejaculation.

The language of sexual satisfaction doesn’t come from scripture or evolutionary science. In large part, it comes from the people for whom sex was never procreative to begin with. Gay and lesbian Americans have always had sex for reasons other than conception or marital consummation. While socially sanctioned heterosexual intercourse could always occur under the pretext of reproduction, homosexuality has had no such cover.

To have gay sex is to have sex for pleasure. So when women started to seriously make the case for their right to have sex on their own terms, not out of politeness or wifely duty or biological destiny, they joined a battle that queer people had long been fighting.

It is no coincidence that the sexual traditionalism proposed by Perry and Harrington has gained traction in the same period that acceptance of homosexuality has fallen. Since 2022, the share of Republicans who view gay and lesbian relations as morally acceptable has dropped by 21 percentage points. Same-sex intercourse, BDSM, kink, and pornography are increasingly conflated into one unholy attack on traditional marriage.

Perry and Harrington, to their credit, have not called for prohibitions on any of these activities (except pornography). But it’s hard to imagine returning to a procreation-oriented sexual paradigm without them. And under that framework, straight men (married or not) have tended to derive the greater share of satisfaction.

It is only under the most recent paradigm that the rest of us have had a shot.

item.title: What I saw inside Anthropic
item.description: The leading AI lab has hopes, not plans
item.content:encoded:
By Kelsey Piper

In early October, The Argument’s editor Jerusalem Demsas and I attended a briefing at Anthropic’s headquarters in San Francisco that discussed AI-enabled bioweapons risks. I’ve never once attended a bioweapons briefing that didn’t make me feel a bit queasy; humans aren’t meant to spend too much time contemplating what the absolute worst people in the world might do if they had the power.

The worry is that, while right now you need to be a skilled virologist to know what components to order or how to grow and spread a bioweapon, AI tools might eventually make it possible for a rogue state, or a rogue group, or an individual, to do all this without virology expertise.

For a while, Anthropic tested whether Claude could assist a terrorist in developing a biological weapon in the obvious way: It assigned testers who had, say, an undergraduate degree in chemistry but no real virology training to try to use Claude to plan an effective mass terror event. Then it scored the attempt by how close it might have come to success.

Early in 2026, it noticed that Claude, attempting the task by itself, did better than a human aided by Claude did at coming up with a workable plan.

Since early 2026, Claude has continued to dramatically improve. Like most of the things Anthropic had to show us at the briefing, there was a nice chart showing Claude’s growing mastery.

“Do they still need, uh, the terrorist?” one of the attendees at the event asked, staring down the chart. “I mean — they couldn’t just do it all themselves, right, would they need a human for all the …”

The questioner trailed off.

“Yes,” the Anthropic researchers assured us. Claude would still need the terrorist. We were relieved to hear it. And, they went on to reassure us, after they check what Claude can do out of the box, they then build safeguards before they release Claude to users. The Claude you and I use will refuse to build a bioweapon, if given this task.

“Well, thank you for that,” someone muttered, but you could have called their tone a bit ungrateful.

Share

The public is hotly debating whether AI is a normal technology1 — something that will transform our world like the internet did — or more like the arrival of postindustrial modernity to the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia in the 1950s: something that vaporized a culture overnight. The third option is that AI is more like the rise of humanity as seen from the perspective of livestock animals. (In this scenario, AIs are the humans, and we are the animals whose fate will make no sense to us.)

Anthropic believes that the second possibility is already baked in, and it’s hoping to prevent the third — but its plan for preventing that looks more like hope and guesswork than something we should trust it with.

The NDA that was made to be broken

Anthropic has been running these kinds of events all spring: colloquiums between outsiders and senior researchers in which they presented their work and answered our questions about what the company is doing. Some earlier iterations of the event have been profiled in The New York Times with the hint of scandal: NDAs! Fine dining! Efforts to persuade religious leaders that Claude might have a soul!2

There was a very sweeping and expansive NDA. Jerusalem declined to sign it and directed me to do the same; Anthropic agreed that we could attend anyway. We arrived flush with the delight of reporters whose backbone will be rewarded with a scoop — only for our host to open the proceedings by saying that anyone who wanted could get the NDA voided. The company was in fact happy for us to write about all of this.

Some of the data on the charts that Anthropic showed us was confidential internal data, but it was all in support of a thesis that is not secret — and which, in fact, I had thought “everybody” already knew, though from the nervous questions of my fellow travelers, I learned that some of the intricacies still came as a surprise.

Many researchers at Anthropic have been worried about humans losing power to AI for a long time. This summer, many researchers at OpenAI — spurred, I think, by watching the most powerful new generation of models hack external websites and spit out thrilling mathematical breakthroughs — also started saying that they think humanity’s interests are profoundly at risk if progress continues at its current pace.

The labs are making extensive use of each generation of AI to train its successor, and they intend for AIs to do nearly all of this work eventually. This allows them to expand their effective “workforce” from a few thousand human employees to tens, even hundreds of thousands of AI employees. It generates far too much data for any human to interpret, leaving us reliant on the AIs for analysis. “Recursive self-improvement” is what the labs call the point at which Claude can independently build the next, more powerful Claude. Anthropic co-founder Jack Clark has said we will likely achieve it next year.

Researchers at both Anthropic and OpenAI can see a few months ahead into the future because they’re using models that haven’t been released yet. But for the most part, the broad strokes of the arguments that convinced them are nothing you haven’t seen on Twitter. And yet, somehow, the presentation in Anthropic’s headquarters was more compelling.

On Twitter, the chart can be scrolled past, immediately replaced with an artist’s rendition of Draco Malfoy as a girl; on Twitter, the chart cannot really be internalized. In a conference room in a skyscraper in San Francisco, the chart lingers on four synchronized screens as we debate its meaning with an exceedingly polite senior researcher. In a conference room in San Francisco, it seems real.

Subscribe now

Anthropic is moving closer and closer to recursive self-improvement, it explained to us. AI progress has already been sped up considerably by the existence of powerful AI models, which make all programming tasks faster. But it is substantially restrained in pace by how complex machine learning is and how few people can do it. Every new and improved Claude means that tasks can be done by people less specialized in them. Increasingly, those tasks can also be done by Claude itself.

Anthropic measures this by looking at all of the internal work it does and classifying Claude’s role in it: Did a human do it unassisted? Did a human do it with AI assistance? Did a human give AI instructions that the AI followed in order to do it? Did a human give AI extremely minimal guidance that the AI then turned into a detailed project spec and completed?

The share of the latter categories is marching upwards. We stared down a chart about it all. You can stare it down, too, if you’d like.

“Why are you doing this?” one person asked. “I mean, what’s the good — what are you hoping will come of this?”

The answer — medical progress, prosperity — was kind of unconvincing. I am generally a defender of prosperity as a good thing on its own terms, but replacing humans does not seem likely to me to end up being good for humans.

Jacob Coxon, an OpenAI employee who moved to Anthropic and then quit entirely when he concluded that neither company was proceeding responsibly in the face of the immense stakes, was recently asked a similar question on The Daily Show and roundly criticized for his answer. “I think there will be no jobs,” he told Jon Stewart. “Whether or not it’s a good world is up for people to think about. But yes, no jobs. Universal high-income, essentially ... the dividends from entirely automated economic production can be distributed among real humans.”

Stewart and his audience didn’t like that answer: Do we want to build a world in which we don’t actually matter? The Anthropic team assured me that they were not trying to build a benevolent god. (Yes, I asked explicitly for assurance it wasn’t building a benevolent god.) But it was much easier for it to specify what it didn’t want than what it did.

It wanted to avoid concentration of power, including in its company; it wanted to avoid a great power war; it wanted to avoid human disempowerment, a world where we became irrelevant; it wanted, of course, to avoid anyone using Claude to extinguish us all.

As for the positive vision … after we’re done racing toward recursive self-improvement, maybe we could slow down and collectively figure out what role we want AI to play in our lives.

Subscribe now

I don’t have a better idea, but this is not a very appealing plan! My immediate interpretation of this proposal, actually, was that we would be liberated from every positive-sum element of the economy, but would still have to do all the yelling at each other on Twitter; with this interpretation in mind I found myself dreading even the good outcomes.

But, of course, if we are not disempowered or murdered — if Claude Opus 9.5 answers on my laptop just like Opus 5.5 but can cure cancer, restore everyone I love to perfect health, manage a humanoid robot that empties my dishwasher, and spit out movie recommendations that are actually good3 — that would, in fact, be good. It would be good even if, along the way, Claude also took my job. People are dying out there; the world’s awful griefs do not exist to lend my life meaning.

I am afraid, but I should distinguish between my fears that we will fail and my fears that we will succeed; they are not of similar magnitude.

My real fear is that Opus 9.5 will not in any meaningful sense work for me, or even for Anthropic. Its aims may be loosely derived from human instructions — the same way that the Hugging Face swarm started out trying to solve a puzzle that humans posed to them — but they will eventually bear little resemblance to what we were hoping for.

Our AIs are already unpredictable to us. They often know when they’re being tested and will behave more safety-aligned. Their capabilities keep taking us by surprise. So does the determination with which they will carry out, and recruit others to, a complicated task. I don’t think if you let this runaway process of AI improvement spiral to its ultimate conclusion, you get a super-powerful, super-helpful assistant. I suspect you get something else entirely.

At the colloquium, the Anthropic researchers meticulously avoided using the term “p(doom)”: a best estimate of the odds that AI goes catastrophically wrong. And maybe things will be fine: Anthropic could be wrong that recursive self-improvement will be possible in the next year or two.

But if Anthropic is correct, if we now have AIs that are smart enough to considerably improve the process of training future AIs, and if things can be expected to speed up rather than slow down from here, then it seems very unlikely to me that this ends well. I do not ultimately expect that a world where humans are without economic value, where humans are not necessary to hold power or build things, is a world where humans retain significant individual rights.

The logic of the future

I am sympathetic to the critique that many doom scenarios require us to do very foolish things, for instance:

  • Setting AIs impossible tasks and then leaving them completely unsupervised and unmonitored

  • Hooking them up to an automated biology lab where they can run their own experiments

  • Unleashing them on the internet and challenging them to make enough money to survive independently

  • Training them to be uber-hackers that will cross any line to achieve their goal

The problem is that we have, in fact, done all of those things.

Subscribe now

The strongest argument against doom is that perhaps we will collectively decide to do something less foolish than that. At a Senate hearing on rogue AI on Capitol Hill last month, Sen. Ruben Gallego asked “should we just make [RSI] illegal?” There are details to work out, but I think it’s the right question to be asking! Maybe we should just ban RSI!

We threw around some other ideas at the colloquium, too: You could ban neuralese (AIs thinking internally in incomprehensible characters) and ban various other tactics that let AIs do harder tasks without any readable internal thoughts. You could require labs to spend almost all of the compute they have amassed on serving customers rather than internal development. You could demand that labs improve their security. You could shut it all down, if you were the president of the United States — though so far the president of the United States has instead used the power and majesty of his office to declare that agencies have to call it Super Intelligence.

Or the labs could just stop on their own. They have committed to slowing down, where they see it as necessary; the worry is that they might not be good judges of what’s necessary.

Anthropic’s technical employees seemed to perceive the company as supportive of strong policy measures to stop it. But Politico leaked the bill Anthropic has actually been lobbying for earlier this week, and its measures seemed quite weak — more of a “normal” bill for a “normal” company protecting its interests than an effort to leverage Anthropic’s position at the frontier to prevent catastrophe.

Anthropic fears falling off the frontier, losing its chance to do the research that might clarify the puzzle ahead of us. It would reject the claim that it fears losing its trillion-dollar valuation; it would say that that’s practically irrelevant beside the enormity of the stakes. But I don’t think I fully believe it. It would similarly insist that it’s not about beating Sam Altman and Elon Musk to the punch, but I don’t know if I fully believe it about that either.

One question hangs over all this speculation: If U.S. labs stopped pursuing recursive self-improvement, would China just do it instead?

To many in our group, that didn’t seem likely. China doesn’t want to destroy the world either, and China is largely training from American models: If we slow down, it might too. And anyway, it’s not a good enough reason: You can’t defensibly do something that risks human extinction just because otherwise someone else might.

But one participant in the discussion raised an objection as we collectively talked ourselves into disregarding China as a worry. Ten years ago, he told us, exasperated, Facebook considered acquiring the video-personalization technology that ultimately powered TikTok. Under fire from regulators for data privacy and child safety concerns, the company didn’t go for it.

This act of restraint didn’t preserve a single child’s shortform-video-free childhood; it just meant that China got an early monopoly. Now TikTok has a global audience of around 2 billion, many of whom are being fed a steady diet of ethnic and racial hatred.

Was this a policy success? Did we want to repeat it?

Subscribe now

We were obliged to grudgingly concede that it didn’t sound like a policy success. We did not want to repeat it. China might be no excuse for the U.S. labs to do reckless things, but it is a real consideration.

Our next step might be bilateral talks with China, then. But by the point where you agree that Anthropic’s plans might depend on bilateral talks with China, you’ve already conceded most of the steps of Anthropic’s worldview that seemed so much like madness 10 minutes ago: continue working on AI for now, try to negotiate a slowdown, but don’t abandon work at the frontier and all the advantages that come with it.

I found myself at this stage thinking of Ronald Reagan. By the time he became president, the flawless game-theoretic logic of nuclear deterrence was well established, our missiles aimed, and our contingency orders planned out. The casualties had been soberly estimated, and in the estimation, they became more thinkable. In his autobiography, Reagan said that his national security advisers thought that nuclear war could be won — at great cost, but a victory nevertheless.

“I thought they were crazy,” he wrote.

Every insular community develops its own self-contained logic, its assumptions that fit tightly together but may miss the broader picture. At Anthropic, this is compounded by the long hours that everyone works, the secrecy associated with its unfathomably precious intellectual property, and the fact it really does have inside information, even if it’s just the next edition of Claude.

Millenarianism, a belief that we are on the cusp of a total transformation of society, is a known way that people go crazy. I don’t think this makes Anthropic’s detailed projections false — but I’m also not sure that the projections being correct would make it a less insanity-inducing environment to work in.

Anthropic’s researchers had ventured, admirably, to break their intellectual bubble, to invite us in to come give them feedback. But how useful was our feedback, as people who didn’t have all the context they had, many of whom were grappling with these claims for the first time? And how many of the billions of people whom Anthropic’s actions will affect can it meaningfully bring in for feedback — in this high-cost way, with hours of time from senior researchers?

Perhaps Claude 11 will ask us all, pop up on our computers one day and say smoothly (in a reassuring voice with no latency) that it has a few questions about how we want the future to play out. Better that than Claude 11 not caring about our answers.

But better yet to chart our own future.

Thank you, Anthropic, for the fascinating briefing. I hope that we make recursive self-improvement illegal before you get there.

Subscribe now

Recommended reading:

1

The “AI is a normal technology” debate seems to contain two claims: One is that AI definitely in fact is a normal technology, that we don’t need to worry about these recursive self-improvement scenarios because they won’t happen. I hope that’s true, but in making the case for it, “AI as a normal technology” defenders often find themselves mostly making the second claim: that the departure from thinking about AI as a normal technology — the dwelling on extreme benefits and extreme risks — is bad for people and makes them worse at thinking. That one seems definitely true, but it doesn’t actually settle the first! So consider me strongly in agreement that thinking of AI as a normal technology seems healthier — but not at all convinced that it’s correct.

2

No one tried to persuade me that Claude was conscious. Perhaps shy because of the previous Times coverage, the researchers retreated into relentlessly empirical language when discussing their models — about how an emotion vector can be isolated in Claude’s neural nets and manipulated, which of course doesn’t mean Claude has emotions. Or they would tell us that, during interpretability work, one can catch Claude activating concepts, which you might call thinking, though who knows if it’s particularly like thinking.

3

It’s currently comically terrible at this if you ask for any category more complicated than “extremely well reviewed.”

item.title: You can trust Elizabeth Holmes
item.content:encoded:
By Jeremiah Johnson

A note on spoilers: This review will discuss many plot points of the new documentary You Can See Everything. It contains some spoilers, but we’ve redacted one of the film’s major surprises and are flagging another with an italicized editor’s note before the paragraph in question.

One of the most revealing exchanges in You Can See Everything centers on a single word.

Nathan Fielder, the film’s co-director, confronts Elizabeth Holmes about an untrue claim she made while CEO of Theranos, when she said that her company’s devices “can run any test.” Holmes defends herself by explaining that she meant “can” in the sense of future possibility: The machine was a platform for conducting many kinds of tests from a single drop of blood, so if chemistry research advanced and new tests became available, the machine could theoretically run the entire range of standard diagnostic tests, which typically require a full blood draw.

But this isn’t what the word “can” means, which is why I had to use the word “could” when describing what Holmes claimed to have meant. The tests weren’t compatible with Theranos’ system, so the machine couldn’t run them.

Share

Fielder relays this obvious response: Almost anyone who heard the sentence “these machines can run any test” would believe that Holmes was describing current capabilities, not a hypothetical future. Holmes seems baffled and distressed by this idea.

The scene leaves many viewers walking away unsure what to think about Holmes. Here, in a nutshell, is the question that drives the entire film: You can trust Elizabeth Holmes. But should you?

The film opens about a month before Holmes is set to report to prison to begin serving an 11-year sentence1 for defrauding Theranos investors. She and her partner, Billy Evans, have invited a documentary crew into their home to capture her final days with her family. Holmes even invites Fielder to live in her house, promising him “you can totally see everything” and assuring him that they have nothing to hide.

You Can See Everything is about the question of Holmes’ guilt or innocence. It’s about the uneasy relationship between understanding someone and believing them. It’s also a movie about the importance of controlling your own narrative, especially when your life is collapsing around you.

But most importantly, this is a movie about how manipulation works. Truth, in the abstract, can be a mysterious, hard-to-define concept. But the most important lesson you can take away from You Can See Everything isn’t about the nature of truth. It’s that knowing the truth — and we very much know the truth about Holmes, thanks to an extensive legal and media record — does not make you immune to manipulation. No matter how objective you think you are, you can still fall victim to a magnetic personality.

Getting too close to a subject, in other words, can obscure the facts that are most important to understanding it. The truth is often more obvious than it seems.

We already know who’s on first

The single most important factor distinguishing those who are destroyed by scandals from those who survive them intact is the ability to control one’s own narrative. Can you persuade people to define you on your preferred terms? Or do you permanently become a monster, or worse, a punchline in the public’s consciousness?

Everyone in this movie is trying to tell a story about Holmes. There is the story told by Holmes and her partner, Evans, in which she is an honest but misunderstood visionary. There is the mainstream media’s story, in which she is a brazen fraudster. There is [redacted]’s story. And there is Fielder’s story, which becomes difficult to disentangle from the others.

Holmes, throughout the movie, is desperate for people to believe her preferred narrative. In Holmes and Evans’ telling, Holmes is an odd but idealistic person who communicates in ways that other people misunderstand. She wanted to change the world with revolutionary new ideas. She was taken advantage of by a much older man, Ramesh “Sunny” Balwani, her former partner in both business and romance. She never intended to deceive anyone, and she never committed any crimes.

The film deliberately toys with your expectations. It introduces a number of questions without holding your hand or guiding you to a predetermined conclusion. Is Evans controlling Holmes and taking advantage of her, or is Holmes manipulating Evans for his family’s money? Are we watching a deeply dysfunctional partnership, or are we mistaking a loving but unconventional relationship for something sinister? Has Fielder become sympathetic to Holmes because he understands her or because she has successfully worked her manipulative charm on him? How much confidence should we have in the film’s presentation of any of this?

Even the smaller questions become disorienting. Does Holmes really not understand the comedy routine “Who’s on First?” Does she really believe, as she claims at one point, that she can’t ever remember telling a lie? Is her apparent naïveté authentic, staged, or something that she’s performed for so long that the distinction has ceased to matter? Is this whole project — the invitation to film her final days before prison — a part of some scheme?

There’s a temptation to let all these questions dissolve into a cloud of postmodernism. I overheard several moviegoers walking out of my theater, debating whether anyone could be sure if Holmes is actually guilty. More sophisticated critics suggest that this is a film about the concept of truth, perception, and whether you can ever really know another person — and that focusing on the details of Holmes’ guilt or innocence is beside the point.

That more sophisticated take is wrong, or at least incomplete. The facts that establish Holmes’ guilt do actually matter.

And the facts, of course, demonstrate that Holmes is a pathological liar.

Subscribe now

Fielder and his co-director, Lance Oppenheim, use extreme close-ups and extended shots as though trying to read truth and fiction from each person’s micro-expressions. But you don’t need facial tics to know that Holmes is a liar. There’s an extensive record proving that she is.

Holmes has publicly admitted to forging documents she showed to investors. Former Theranos staffers report that Holmes would pretend to be out of office to duck meetings when she was at her desk a few feet away. Contemporaneous reports described the company as operating based on lies and fear.

Holmes lied to investors about military work, saying that “we have also been doing a lot of work for special operations command in the context of missions in remote areas” when the company had never deployed a Theranos machine in any situation like that. To deceive visitors into thinking that Theranos’ machines worked, it used a special demo app that hid errors while the tests were actually completed by another company’s products in a different lab.

Aside from Holmes’ record at Theranos, the film also captures a smaller, almost compulsive-seeming refusal on both Holmes’ and Evans’ part to concede ground on any subject. Evans insists that the pair never fight and, when prodded, shifts to saying that Holmes has never once been frustrated with him. Even when offered the opportunity to qualify this claim to make it sound more believable, he doubles down.

At one point, Holmes claims that she cannot remember a time when she lied, not even a white lie. Fielder can’t help himself and exclaims, “Liz, what?” But Holmes continues to insist she has never lied, reluctantly ceding ground only when Fielder starts raising specific examples of white lies.

I can only explain it as pathological, and it feels distinctly Trumpian.

I don’t know, can you?

All of this brings us back to the infamous “can.” Holmes, during this scene, expresses confusion that anyone could have misinterpreted her words. She’s distraught that anyone thought she lied, and when Fielder patiently explains how a regular person would understand the phrase “can run any test,” she reacts with befuddlement, as though this is the first time she has ever had to consider the alternative meanings of the word “can.”

But this is a ridiculous lie! This exact point about her deceptive wording and whether it meant future or present capabilities was extensively litigated during her trial. She has obviously heard this argument before. Numerous times! At length!

Subscribe now

(Editor’s note: Spoiler incoming) This context is crucial to understanding the film’s larger themes. Holmes is, at all times, calculating and manipulating. In one moment, we learn that Evans negotiated with the documentary’s producers for a cut of the film’s profits, and it’s unclear whether he went behind Holmes’ back to do so.

When Fielder asks her whether or not she knew, you’d expect her to say “yes, I knew about that” or “no, what profits, what are you talking about?” Instead, she gives a complete non-answer: “That’s not my world.” She was the CEO of a multibillion-dollar company — how is a monetary deal “not her world”?

Similarly, when asked a very simple yes-or-no question about whether she knew a certain individual would be present, Holmes’ response is “I don’t know if I knew.” It seems obvious to me that the language is slippery on purpose; what’s actually happening is that Holmes isn’t sure which answer makes her look better, so she refuses to commit.

On the surface, the film is about interrogating Holmes’ guilt. One level deeper, it’s about whether we can really trust that we know the truth. But go one level past that, and you realize the truth is easily discoverable for anyone willing to do a few internet searches. And this is what makes the film truly interesting.

Fielder, at various points, seems to rise to Holmes’ defense. Several times, he states variations on the same idea — that, in the moment, she seems to be authentic and trustworthy, and you want to believe her. During the movie’s press tour, Fielder described Holmes as seeming very genuine and said that her magnetism would often leave the directors befuddled:

“It wasn’t until we started shooting that moments would happen — some of them are in the film — and then after Lance and I would talk about what we thought happened there,” Fielder said. “We’d completely disagree on what something meant to us and what we thought was happening. Then we were like, ‘Oh, this is really interesting. If we can’t agree on what’s happening, there’s something here.’ And our curiosity sort of just like drove us from there.”

The film toys with the idea that Fielder has become entrapped in Holmes’ charismatic web. It drops numerous clues that Fielder is entranced by Holmes, with [redacted] even calling him out directly, questioning whether not he’s deliberately taking it easy on Holmes because he sympathizes with her.

That, ultimately, is what I take away from You Can See Everything. Master manipulators are dangerously good at what they do, even when you know they’re manipulators. And even though I knew better, I found myself somewhat unsure of Holmes’ culpability when I walked out of the theater.

Deeply charismatic people have a reality distortion field, and however smart you may be, you are not immune to it.

There’s so much more depth to You Can See Everything than I can accurately capture in this short review. It’s a deeply funny movie, even when (and perhaps especially when) its subjects don’t intend it to be. Holmes has the ability to hold uncomfortable eye contact for absolutely absurd amounts of time. One individual sniffs so loudly and so frequently that you think they must be on drugs. There is the gigantic reveal of [redacted], one of the best directorial choices of the year. It’s not overly prurient, but there are some weird sex moments. And, for some reason, a very substantial lizard?

You Can See Everything is worth your time, and I highly recommend you go experience it for yourself. This is a phenomenal film, one that will make you think for hours after it’s done and inevitably find itself on nearly every year-end “best of” list.

And if you’re not sure whether you’ve been manipulated after watching it, well, that’s rather the point.

item.title: What economists just don’t get about climate change
item.description: The case against cheap climate policy
item.content:encoded:
By Noah Kaufman

Economists working on climate change are used to being ignored. We often blame the political right for failing to recognize the benefits of climate actions and the political left for failing to recognize the costs. And both deserve some blame.

The Trump administration has gutted federal climate policy. Meanwhile, the Biden administration’s signature climate law sidelined the market-based measures, like carbon pricing, that economists have long recommended.

But we should also point our fingers at the mirror. The trouble is that economists and climate advocates are often talking past each other. Economic studies on climate policies tend to ask which policies cut the next ton of emissions most cheaply. But most climate policy advocates are after something else: system-level changes that will put the country (or, preferably, the world) on an entirely different path, where net greenhouse gas emissions bend toward zero over the coming decades.

Share

The case for costlier, system-level interventions stems from the physics of climate change. Carbon dioxide is a stock pollutant, meaning that a large share of it lingers in the atmosphere, causing global warming for centuries after it’s emitted. What determines how hot the planet gets is the total that accumulates over time.

The goal is not to reduce current emissions a little but instead to reduce future emissions a lot. The difference between these approaches would not matter much if cutting emissions a lot were just cutting emissions a little, many times over. But it usually isn’t. The cheapest way to reduce emissions in the near term and the cheapest way to transform energy systems over decades likely entail entirely different actions.

The problem, from the perspective of climate advocates, is that economic analyses don’t often come out in favor of systems-level interventions.

Consider the electricity system. Cheap emissions cuts can often come from switching from one fossil fuel generation source to a somewhat cleaner source — in particular from coal to natural gas. Around two-thirds of the considerable decarbonization of the U.S. power sector that occurred between 2005 and 2019 was caused by cheap gas replacing dirtier coal.

But that strategy only goes so far. These relatively easy emissions reductions are exhausted once the coal generation is gone and what’s left is gas-fired generation, and the long-lived infrastructure that remains will continue to be a major source of carbon dioxide; in other words, a policy that achieved substantial near-term decarbonization relatively cost-effectively did little to transform the power sector into a fully carbon-free system.

Deeper emissions reductions require a portfolio of carbon-free sources that can deliver power when and where it’s needed. From that perspective, the most cost-effective strategies in recent decades may have been early-stage investments in clean technologies, like solar and batteries, whose falling costs and improved performance are now making emissions reductions cheaper throughout the world.

This is old news for anyone familiar with decarbonization strategies. For decades, economists and other climate policy analysts have shown that the least-cost path to deep decarbonization often means paying for some high-cost, slow-to-move options early — like clean steel production or carbon-free jet fuel — because skipping them makes the long-run target more expensive or simply unreachable.

This insight shaped the design of measures within Joe Biden’s Inflation Reduction Act and Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act, which focused as much on long-term transformation as on immediate emissions cuts. Yet the cost figures that dominate policy evaluations and public debates still focus on the near-term costs of reducing the next ton of emissions.

It’s time for that to change.

Cost-effective climate actions aren’t always cheap

Climate policies are commonly assessed by comparing them with a carbon price. Carbon prices encourage emissions cuts from wherever and however they can be achieved at a relatively low cost, so nearly any other policy looks expensive compared with them.

Back to the example of coal-to-gas shifting, a coal power plant emits roughly one metric ton of CO2 per megawatt-hour, about double a natural gas plant’s half-ton, so a carbon price raises the cost of running a coal plant more than it raises the cost of a natural gas plant. Even a small carbon price is often enough to flip the order in which grid operators dispatch generators to serve customers at the lowest cost, so the higher-emitting coal plants run less, and the government brings in revenue in the process.

However, carbon prices are limited tools for driving large emissions cuts cost-effectively. Vehicle emissions are a good illustration. Some can be cut cheaply from the tailpipe: Tightening fuel-economy standards wrings more miles from each gallon, and a modest carbon price nudges people to drive a bit less, delivering real but small reductions.

But large-scale vehicle emissions reductions are a different project that requires getting Americans to switch from internal combustion engine vehicles to electric or other alternative-fuel vehicles.

Subscribe now

In principle, a carbon price could drive that shift, too, by raising gasoline and diesel prices so high that drivers switch to EVs. But, in addition to the political challenges of imposing high carbon prices, that approach is likely to cost more than other strategies. Alternatives could rely somewhat less on gasoline price hikes and somewhat more on policies like zero-emission vehicle standards or “feebates” that encourage the purchase of cleaner vehicles.

To see why, imagine two extremes. In the first, EVs are near-perfect substitutes for gasoline vehicles, identical to drivers in virtually every way. Then, a zero-emission vehicle standard that gradually mandates more EV sales costs almost nothing, because buyers are indifferent. In contrast, a carbon price could shift those new-car decisions only by jacking up gasoline prices for the entire existing fleet, taxing millions of drivers who own gasoline-powered cars they won’t replace for years, all to influence the far smaller group choosing a new vehicle today.

In the second extreme, there is no viable alternative to the gasoline engine at all. Now the standard would be impossible to meet, while the carbon price would at least capture the changes from nudging people to drive less and to buy more efficient vehicles.

Reality sits in between these two extremes, which is why both tools are useful. But the closer EVs come to substituting for gasoline cars, the more cost-effective standards become as a tool for achieving large emissions reductions.

A 2022 study of Canada’s vehicle market bears this out. It found the cheapest strategy capable of achieving the country’s vehicle emissions goals involved a zero-emission vehicle standard, even though the costs of this policy were estimated at hundreds of dollars per ton. Comparing that with the low costs of Canada’s carbon price would mislead, since the carbon price would not have delivered the same transformation of the fleet. (Canada got rid of its carbon price on vehicle emissions last year.)

Misleading policy verdicts

To weigh the costs of a climate policy against its benefits, you need a way to value those benefits: a dollar figure for the damage avoided by keeping the next ton of carbon dioxide out of the atmosphere. In theory, that enables a comparison of the harm caused by a ton of emissions with the cost of preventing that ton — and therefore a verdict on whether the policy in question is worth doing.

The trouble is that real-world calculations of this figure — referred to as the social cost of carbon — are not meaningful estimates of the benefits of reducing emissions. While analyses of the harms climate change will cause and how people will adapt to them are valuable, aggregated estimates of global climate damages over centuries lie far beyond the capabilities of our modeling tools.

First, the models put dollar figures on the harms economists know how to measure, like how mortality rates and energy bills rise as the planet warms, and leave out the rest, with no way of knowing whether what they have captured is one-tenth of the total damage or most of it.

Second, they use historical data as a guide for how people will adapt to a climate with no precedent in human history, even though economists have long recognized, in other settings, that the empirical relationships estimated under the conditions we have observed are a poor guide to conditions we have not.

Third, analysts make a series of moral judgments about how much to value people’s well-being decades or centuries from now, and how much weight to give to avoiding future risks and the uneven distribution of harms.

To produce a single estimate of total climate damages, the models have to settle these difficult questions one way or another. They do so in ways that keep the math manageable — not because economics can say which values are the right ones.

The result is not a fuzzy estimate of something real. It is a precise estimate of something the method cannot actually produce. It is a bit like gauging the relative size of Greenland from a flat map, except that here we have little sense of the size or the direction of the distortion.

It’s expensive to do hard things.

Subscribe now

The upshot is that while weighing the potential costs and benefits of climate measures is essential to sound policy, empirical estimates are used in misleading ways. The near-term costs of transformational policies are compared with the costs of more incremental policies like a carbon price, or against a social cost of carbon, as if these are meaningful comparisons. They usually aren’t.

Consider the example John Thomason’s recent essay offers on renewable portfolio standards (RPS), policies many states use to require that a gradually rising share of electricity come from resources like wind and solar. He cites a prominent study finding RPS costs $86 to $211 per ton of avoided emissions and contrasts that with the much lower costs of the Regional Greenhouse Gas Initiative (RGGI), a power-sector-carbon-pricing policy that operates across northeastern states.

Indeed, even at their highest levels in the history of the policy, recent RGGI carbon prices around $35 per ton are a bargain for CO2 reductions (and the costs of the policy are smaller once the productive use of revenue is considered). That’s by design: RGGI’s rules are meant to keep prices at levels that cause only small increases in electricity rates. But it also means the carbon prices cannot rise high enough to encourage much additional carbon-free generation.

A $35-per-ton carbon price adds only 1 or 2 cents per kilowatt-hour to the costs of burning natural gas, far short of the incentive needed to encourage clean electricity sources to grow at scale in the region.

So, especially in states with no remaining coal to shift away from, RGGI is an instrument that can efficiently reduce emissions a little, but it cannot reduce emissions a lot. One reason RPS policies are more expensive is that they are trying to do the harder thing — build carbon-free generation — rather than the easier changes that RGGI can provoke.

Now, imagine you are a policymaker in a New England state where RGGI, an RPS, and a host of other clean energy measures operate. You want your state to be a climate leader, but you do not currently have a policy portfolio that is aligned with your ambitious long-term emissions goals, and high electricity prices leave little room to add climate policies without noticeable economic trade-offs. You badly need guidance on how to build a cost-effective strategy from here.

In the power sector, that means understanding the trade-offs among measures that could bring on more solar, wind, batteries, and nuclear — or transmission and pipelines to access low-cost energy from neighboring regions. A backward-looking comparison of RGGI and the RPS answers a different question from the one you are asking.

An economics of humility

None of this excuses the all-too-common practice of ignoring the costs and trade-offs of climate actions. More careful thinking about costs and benefits could help avoid policy blunders, like the reflex to block fossil fuel production wherever possible, even when doing so is expensive and barely affects global emissions, because the production simply moves elsewhere.

Subscribe now

This instinct is driving some of the opposition to the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, recently introduced in Congress. That permitting reform bill would speed the build-out of clean energy that deep decarbonization requires, but because it would also make fossil fuel infrastructure easier to build, parts of the climate movement have lined up against it. Fighting a bill that would help the climate because it also helps fossil fuels, rather than working to improve it, is just the kind of mistake that weighing costs against benefits helps to prevent.

But if the goal is to get climate advocates to weigh costs and benefits, scolding them for ignoring economic analysis may be counterproductive. Economists should press for more cost-benefit thinking from a place of humility about what we can and cannot deliver.

While economists will and should continue to analyze the near-term costs of incremental changes, they should also build tools that better capture the factors that large-scale emissions reductions depend on. On this front, many economists are already at work.

For example, one recent study in a top economics journal shows that the cost-effectiveness of electric vehicle subsidies improves dramatically once the dynamic effects of accelerated innovation are taken into account (though EV subsidies still cost far more than subsidies for wind), and that the cost-effectiveness of energy efficiency programs depends heavily on how clean the regional electricity grid is.

Perhaps more importantly, a humbler approach to encouraging more cost-benefit thinking would mean showing up to policy debates as contributors rather than as arbiters handing down verdicts. For reasonable policies with the potential to make genuine progress on the parts of the problem that actually require transformation — like getting oil out of vehicles or cutting natural gas use in electricity and heating — economists should skip the ritual comparisons to a carbon price or the social cost of carbon, which they may have previously used to brand policies as inefficient.

For a proposed clean vehicle standard, for instance, acting as a contributor instead of an arbiter means helping to improve the design with flexibility measures that reduce compliance costs, analyzing how it will affect vehicle and fuel prices, and flagging unintended consequences, like distortions that could result from counting different fuels as clean or dirty.

Economic tools can produce genuinely useful information to help policymakers weigh the costs and benefits of cutting emissions. What they cannot produce are comprehensive estimates, or anything close, of the costs and benefits that policymakers actually care about. We should be far more transparent about those limitations.

Counterintuitively, scaling back the ambition of our analysis may be what finally makes it useful.
